transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-07-28 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Jonas Meyer (Redwood SE), Maya Rios (Eclipse CTO), Samir Patel (Platform Eng), Leah Ortiz (Security), Diego Ramos (Infra)

Auto-summary: quick pod style run through of offline bundle delivery and a deep tunnel into runtime perf knobs, lots of focus on KV eviction and how quant affects tail latency.

[00:00] Lena: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about 70 minutes, we'll do a quick agenda then jonas will jump into the runtime bits, and then we'll cover the offline handoff and license rotation.
[00:20] Maya: great thanks lena, we want to make sure the airgap handoff doesn't introduce a long lead for drivers and that we can rotate license keys without service interruption.
[00:35] Jonas: cool, i'll start with a high level of the runtime — we run a GPU-optimized engine, supports int8/4 quant, continuous batching, and prefix KV cache; for on-prem airgap the key questions are: how do you ship artifacts, how do you sign them, and how do we warm the KV cache without internet.
[01:05] Samir: on our side, we have an internal staging rack, no outbound egress; we can accept tarballs via removable media, and we have an HSM for key material. So the manifest/checksum process is crucial.
[01:30] Jonas: yes, recommended pattern — Redwood creates a signed manifest, accompanying tarball with model weights, runtime packages, and a driver bundle. We provide a detached signature and a SHA256 checksum. You verify signature against our pubkey shipped on a separate channel (we can provision via PGP or hardware token).
[02:05] Leah: okay are you proposing sending any keys with the bundle?
[02:10] Lena: no we won't include active license keys inside the tarball. We'll do an offline license activation flow: you receive an activation token signed by Redwood, then you import it into your HSM and do an attestation handshake during the first boot of the private control plane.
[02:40] Maya: can you walk through the license rotation? we need to be able to rotate monthly without needing to re-airgap every time.
[02:50] Jonas: yep — rotation plan: we provide a rotation tool that accepts a new signed license blob; you upload that blob to the HSM and call an offline rotate API on the control plane. The control plane doesn't need outbound network — it validates the signature with our public key already provisioned. We also support multi-signed rotation for orgs that require a second approver.
[03:20] Diego: and for the GPU drivers — we need kernel module signing for our SUSE kernels, plus we require FIPS-signed firmware. How do you coordinate driver versions?
[03:35] Jonas: we bundle a set of tested driver/firmware combinations per platform (NVIDIA 4xx/5xx series, AMD MI200 family etc). For airgap we provide signed pkg repos and kernel module .signed artifacts. We also include a driver-compat matrix. You'll test the bundle in staging; if a driver needs to be swapped we provide delta bundles to reduce transfer size.
[04:05] Maya: that sounds good. Now on the runtime perf side, we're trying to meet 60ms p50 on short chat prompts and sustain 1200 tok/s for embedding pipelines. Where do batching and quantization come in here?
[04:25] Jonas: ok two axes: batching increases throughput but increases per-request latency if you wait to fill a batch. For p50 targets you can keep micro-batches of 1-4 with aggressive scheduling; for throughput runs you go to batch sizes 16-64 depending on model and sequence lengths.
[04:55] Jonas: quantization — INT8 or 4-bit reduces memory and can increase throughput by 1.8-3x, but you may see tail latency spikes if kernel code paths for quant differ on certain sequence lengths. We ran a few INT8 kernels that produced slightly higher p99 when KV cache misses trigger expensive re-compact paths.
[05:30] Samir: what's your recommendation for KV eviction? Our workload has a mix of user chat sessions and long-running embeddings. We don't want to blow up memory.
[05:40] Jonas: default is LRU with a prefetched warmup window. For airgap you can't prime the cache from live traffic easily, so strategy: 1) provide a synthetic warmup script that replays a small set of representative prefixes during initial bring-up; 2) use segmented caches — one partition pinned for high-value keys (session tokens) and an LRU for the rest; 3) use weighted eviction based on token frequency.
[06:15] Leah: are there durability guarantees if a node reboots?
[06:20] Jonas: KV is in-memory for latency; we checkpoint hot keys to a local encrypted snapshot periodically (configurable interval). On restart the control plane can seed the cache from snapshot. For strict durability you should persist to encrypted local SSD and import snapshot at boot.
[06:45] Maya: what about the risk of cache poisoning or stale keys with offline rotation?
[06:50] Jonas: rotate the cache snapshot alongside the license rotation; the license tool includes a cache-seed verification step which flags mismatched versions. We also sign checkpoint metadata.
[07:10] [Short crosstalk] Diego: ok good.
[07:25] Jonas: now i'll share micro-bench results we ran in-house — note these numbers are from our lab on an A100-ish node: FP16 baseline p50 ~45ms on the model you referenced, INT8 optimized p50 ~33ms, throughput increase ~2.1x at batch 32. However p99 went from 210ms to 285ms in INT8 on long sequences due to kernel fallback on certain attention blocks.
[08:05] Samir: so it's a tradeoff — we can get cost/throughput benefits but we need to manage fallbacks. Can you mitigate the p99?
[08:15] Jonas: yes: we recommend hybrid profiles — run INT8 for short token paths and fall back to FP16 for long contexts or for requests flagged as latency-critical. Our runtime supports per-request model variant routing — you can pin certain endpoints to FP16. Also we can apply KV-aware batching: if a request causes a cache miss and triggers an expensive path, we throttle similar requests into a separate queue.
[09:00] Maya: that per-request routing, does it complicate billing/metrics?
[09:05] Lena: no the console will show per-route token breakdown, model variant, and cost. We'll expose a tag so you can attribute cost to FP16 vs INT8.
[09:25] Leah: security question — how are keys stored on the node? we have to meet SOC2 plus internal controls.
[09:35] Jonas: we support KMS integrations and HSMs. For airgap we provide an HSM onboarding script that writes the Redwood public key into a secure module; license blobs are sealed and only unsealed by HSM. We also log attestation events to a local audit log that you can ship out-of-band for compliance.
[10:05] Maya: let's talk about the actual handoff — step by step.
[10:10] Lena: step 1 Redwood builds and signs bundles and generates a manifest + detached signature. Step 2 we upload to a secure drop (or provide physical media). Step 3 Eclipse verifies the signature and checksum, and runs the preflight install script which validates kernel module signatures and driver checks. Step 4 license activation: import activation blob to HSM and run offline activate. Step 5 warmup: run synthetic seed script to populate KV cache.
[10:55] Diego: for verification, can we have an automated verifier script with exit codes? manual checks are error prone.
[11:05] Jonas: yes we provide a verifier that returns structured exit codes and generates a verification report. We'll include a 'verify.sh' that checks signatures, checksums, package versions, kernel module signatures and driver compatibility.
[11:30] Samir: bandwidth/transfer size — our removable media is limited to 10TB, but we want smallest delta. How big are these bundles typically?
[11:40] Jonas: full model + runtime can be ~1.2TB for larger models; we provide quantized deltas and shared runtime libs to reduce to ~350-600GB depending on quant. We also support chunked transfer with resume.
[12:05] Maya: for the delta model patches, is there a recommended process for patch signing?
[12:10] Lena: yes each delta is signed and the manifest chains to the base manifest; the verifier verifies the chain. We also publish a release notes artifact that records kernel/driver combos.
[12:35] Jonas: quick note on batching knobs in the control plane — you can set max_batch_latency_ms and max_batch_size; we recommend conservative max_batch_latency_ms=12ms for interactive workloads and larger for throughput. Use adaptive batch sizing for variable sequence lengths.
[13:05] Samir: what's the impact on memory for larger batch sizes when using INT8 vs FP16?
[13:12] Jonas: INT8 halves activation memory in many cases but some kernels allocate temporary buffers that don't quantize as well — so be conservative, perhaps 1.6x memory efficiency in practice.
[13:35] [Ambient noise, brief pause]
[13:55] Leah: compliance — do you provide audit logs for license activations and rotation? we need proof for audits.
[14:00] Lena: yes activation, rotation, and verification events are stored in the local audit log; for airgap you can export signed audit bundles via USB or scp to your SIEM. Every event is signed by the runtime using the local key, which you can verify against the HSM root.
[14:30] Maya: ok last part — pilots and success criteria. We want a pilot that proves: offline handoff works end-to-end, we can hit 60ms p50 on short prompts with 95% of traffic, and that license rotation is non-disruptive. Can we scope that?
[14:50] Lena: yes proposed pilot: 2-week on-site pilot using a single 4-GPU node, run synthetic load to validate p50/p99 and KV warmup, run license rotate twice. Deliverables: runbook + verification report + perf spreadsheet.
[15:10] Jonas: i'll run the INT8/FP16 micro-bench and include scripts so you can run locally. We'll also include the synthetic warmup set and a recommended eviction policy file.
[15:30] Maya: good. We'll review the runbook and book the staging window.
[15:40] [wrap up] Lena: recap — i'll send the signed runbook + manifest template; jonas will send perf scripts; eclipse will provide staging access window; leah will confirm HSM compatibility. Next checkpoint in one week to confirm access and two-week cadence for bench results.
[15:55] Maya: thanks all, appreciate it.

End of transcript.

References mentioned: signed manifest (link to runbook placeholder), verifier script (verify.sh), perf spreadsheet (link placeholder)
